record.file_problem: The paper is substantially complete. Some figure content and table layout are garbled or flattened in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates SAE-derived neuron activations in language models using interpretability metrics, a different, indirect measure of whether dictionaries recover meaningful sparse features; it does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition as a hypothesis and illustrates crate's intended sparse, axis-aligned representations, but does not measure feature overlap, orthogonality, capacity competition, or one-dimensional feature geometry. The crate-versus-GPT-2 interpretability scores are not rows here because they do not directly measure SAE feature recovery. The SAE interpretability comparisons in Table 3 are the results that bear indirectly on V4.
record.test_reason: Its GPT-2 vs GPT2-SAE comparison is a secondary, indirect V4 test. It uses automated interpretability scores in small GPT-2 models to check whether dictionary features are more interpretable than neurons. The main contribution, the crate architecture, is not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Building sparse coding into the crate architecture improves neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2, at some cost in next-token loss. Post-hoc SAEs on GPT-2 help under the short-context Anthropic metric but not the long-context OpenAI metrics, and that gain declines with depth. Smaller SAE gains on crate are read as crate having 'more optimal' representations.
record.recipe_differences: This is a language-model architecture and interpretability comparison, not the original toy-model superposition method. It builds sparsification into crate and compares against GPT-2 and post-hoc SAEs.
record.method_sensitivity: The SAE comparison varies by interpretability metric: crate-SAE has a negative change under OpenAI TaR and a positive change under Anthropic. The paper also reports that GPT2-SAE Anthropic interpretability decreases with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying SAEs to crate, a model with built-in sparse coding, changes interpretability by -10.2 (OpenAI TaR) and +6.5 (Anthropic), smaller gains than for GPT-2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectures with built-in sparse coding leave less for post-hoc dictionaries to gain in interpretability than standard transformers do.

fits_no_version.finding: crate neurons score more interpretable than GPT-2 MLP neurons, up to 103% relative, across sizes and layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Building sparse coding into the architecture reduces neuron polysemanticity.

record.peer_reviewed: Second Conference on Parsimony and Learning (CPAL 2025), Oral
record.problems: The SAE evidence is based on automated interpretability metrics rather than direct verification of recovered features. Table 3 gives aggregate score changes without specifying their aggregation details or uncertainty. The paper reports metric-dependent and depth-related differences.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's GPT-2-versus-crate neuron interpretability scores (Tables 2, 6, and 7; Figures 6 and 12), SAE metric scores in other tables, and qualitative examples were not extracted as rows because they do not directly measure the V4 feature-recovery claim or add a distinct Table 3 comparison. No results on V1–V3, V5, or V6 were reported.

untested.parts: All: no toy models and no geometry or sparsity transition.
All: capacity is not manipulated and no dedicated-dimension analysis is done.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; only SAE interpretability scores and reconstruction are reported, in 1-3 layer GPT-2 models.
All: no completeness, stability or canonicality tests.

missing.what: Per-layer GPT2-SAE vs GPT-2 scores under the OpenAI random-only and TaR metrics, including drops for 1L (e.g. random-only 8.9 to 2.9)
GPT2-SAE Anthropic interpretability decreases significantly with layer depth
SAE reconstruction recovery scores on GPT-2 of about 82-95% across widths and layers

record.verdict_notes: The V4 evidence is weak and indirect: small 1-3 layer models, LLM-judge scores, and no uncertainty reported. Table 3's GPT-2 OpenAI value conflicts with the prose and Table 6. Superposition is only cited as background.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The study evaluates SAE activation interpretability, not how widely features are distributed across neurons or whether SAE features recover all model features.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether the model's features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: GPT2-SAE
rows.operation_detail: Apply a trained sparse auto-encoder to GPT-2 activations and evaluate the change in interpretability score.
rows.measure: Change in interpretation score after SAE, ρ(gpt2-sae) − ρ(gpt-2)
rows.note: The reported score change is an interpretability proxy for dictionary feature recovery; Table 3 does not specify the aggregation details.
rows.check: Table 3 reports +34.8 under OpenAI TaR, but the Section 5.3 text says GPT2-SAE 'matches GPT-2' under the long-context OpenAI metrics. Table 6 shows mixed per-layer results, e.g. GPT-1L TaR 8.8 vs SAE 5.4. The units of Table 3 (absolute or relative %) are unstated, so read this value with caution. Role is a comparator to the authors' own crate model.
